p88: 88.  The Czech Government further stated that the Hague Convention had expressly reserved matters relating to rights of custody to the courts of the country of the child’s habitual residence and that refusal of return was provided for by way of exceptions in the event of a grave risk to the child. The Czech Government considered that the development of the Court’s case-law, which they outlined, undermined the principle of subsidiarity and ran counter to the aim pursued by the Hague Convention. An “in-depth examination of the entire family situation” would amount to an examination of custody itself, while slowing down the proceedings, even though the passage of time could influence the child where it was possible for him or her to be heard. Fairness would furthermore require that the parent at fault, who bore the burden of proving within a very short space of time the existence of a grave risk in the event of the child’s return, should be deprived of any procedural advantage, rather than being favoured by being able to choose the courts of the country of his or her choice to rule on the merits of custody of the child.
p89: 89.  The Czech Government noted in particular a conflict between the speed required by the Hague Convention and the high standard required in the taking of evidence in the Court’s recent case-law. There was a considerable difference in the assessment of the best interests of the child depending on whether it was a matter of return proceedings before the courts of the country where the child was located or of an examination of the merits of custody by another court, that of the country of habitual residence. Since the States Parties to the European Convention and to the Hague Convention had to comply with their obligations under both frameworks, they required a consistent interpretation and application reconciling those two instruments, bearing in mind that the “Brussels II bis Regulation” was even stricter than the Hague Convention. The database set up by the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law (INCADAT) showed that national courts tended to maintain a strict application of the Hague Convention, in keeping with its purpose. The Czech Government, while advocating a return to the principle of subsidiarity, invited the Grand Chamber to overturn the Chamber judgment and to set limits on the examination of the family situation by courts dealing with a request for return.
p90: 90.  Reunite pointed out that the Hague Convention had been designed to facilitate the protection of children who were victims of wrongful international abduction, on the assumption that, save in exceptional cases, a child’s prompt return was in his or her best interests. Reunite fully agreed with the Court’s summary of the spirit of the Hague Convention in its judgment in Maumousseau and Washington (cited above, § 69). It noted in particular that the Hague Convention, which had been enormously successful in combating international child abduction, was aimed not at the protection of adults but at that of children. It provided for a limited number of exceptions to the child’s prompt return, reserving questions concerning the child’s general long-term situation to the courts of the place of his or her habitual residence. The task of those courts was therefore to carry out an in-depth review of the situation in the child’s interests, unlike the courts of the country where the child was located which, when dealing with a request for return, had to give a ruling following an examination limited to the framework laid down by the Hague Convention.
p91: 91.  While noting that the Court had identified in its case-law key points for the proper functioning of the Hague Convention, Reunite observed that a recent development appeared to require the courts to conduct a more in-depth examination in ruling on the exceptions to the child’s return. It therefore asked the Grand Chamber to clarify the issue of the requirement of an in-depth examination of the entire family situation in the context of the Hague Convention, and to specify that this concerned only the compatibility of the return with the Convention and did not call into question the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of the place of habitual residence on the merits.
